item.title: The Daily Star – David Curley and Mangalkavya: The historian who found Bengal’s past in its poetry
item.description:
Professor David L. Curley (born 1945) has worked with complete dedication on precolonial Bengali literature, especially the Mangalkavya, for close to half a century now. The Mangalkavya are a set of highly charged vernacular texts heralding the extraordinary powers of Bengali goddesses, whose sacred authority must be devoutly recognised. Those who dared to defy it did so at their own peril, in spectacles that served as deterrents to naysayers. Much greater divinely ordained power than that enjoyed by the goddesses was required to contain them. While Brahmanical gods could do so by appropriating them as wives or daughters, Muslim sultans suffered through miracles defying age and chronology and ensuring their destruction, so the narrative goes.

Professor Curley began his pursuit of the goddesses and the literature associated with them after serving in the US Army for a couple of years, including a year in Vietnam. It was his experiences in Vietnam that led to his decision to study the inception of colonial rule in India, having decided while still in Vietnam that his research would never be based solely on British and European sources. Happily, it had to be Bengali and focused primarily on the Mangalkavya. Returning to academia in Chicago and working with medieval Bengali literature, Professor Curley completed his PhD thesis, ‘Rulers and Merchants in 18th Century Bengal’ (1980), under the supervision of Professor Bernard Cohn, renowned as an ‘anthropologist among historians’.
 
David L. Curley, Emeritus Professor.

The thesis was mainly about writing economic history on the basis of religious literature. Historians find the material they look for. Wanting to write a standard and objective economic history and looking for material on prices, production, flows of goods in trade, profits, etc., Professor Curley found some in literature, and that too in a corpus meant to glorify the powers of Bengali goddesses and other local powerholders.

This was in an intellectual context in which the scope of history was being expanded through interdisciplinary research in the social sciences and humanities, with scholars such as Edward Said and Michel Foucault dismantling established structures of power and knowledge. The older historians were still innocently obsessed with looking for hard facts in government data, while literary scholars did not have much sense of history and were yet confident of supplanting it through their novels and other interesting creative works. Professor Curley was thus among the few historians, indeed trailblazers, to study literature closely for writing history. This has become more fashionable now, with lots of smart people, historians or literary scholars, going around claiming the field as their exclusive domain. The more sensible ones are showing considerable respect for each other’s work, speaking while travelling in the same boat, as it were.
 
The cover of Poetry and History: Bengali Mangal-Kābya and Social Change in Precolonial Bengal by David L. Curley, published by Chronicle Books in 2008.

Working on early modern Bengali vernacular texts as historical sources must also have been a pioneering endeavour. Most historians of Bengal prefer to work on sources and archival material from the colonial period. It may sound bizarre, but until recently, few Bengali historians actually worked on the precolonial period. Manuscripts are difficult to access, and published critical editions are rare. The dominant privileging of Persian sources from the Sultanate and Mughal periods might also be scaring them away. Defying these difficulties, Professor Curley’s impressive list of over two dozen research papers is instructive.

Several powerful essays, based on close readings of the versified texts and originating in his doctoral thesis, were subsequently brought together in a book: Poetry and History: Bengali Mangal-Kābya and Social Change in Precolonial Bengal (New Delhi: Chronicle Books, 2008). This writer also had the good fortune to work with Professor Curley, following a serendipitous meeting over the most delicious of kababs and biryani on a typically pleasant winter evening in Kolkata. This led to a fine collaboration over the next decade and a half, which also witnessed, productively, the publication of an edited volume on what else but the deep interstices of literature and history: Literary and Religious Practices in Medieval and Early Modern India (Delhi: Manohar and London: Routledge, 2016).
 
The cover of Literary and Religious Practices in Medieval and Early Modern India, edited by Raziuddin Aquil and David L. Curley and published by Manohar in 2016.

In our times, as always, some people thrive in organised chaos, while others express their concerns quietly. The fine experience of working on the volume with Professor Curley has once again confirmed this writer’s belief that good human beings continue to exist. They work diligently and conscientiously, with a carefully cultivated elegance, encouraging younger colleagues with great affection, noticing politics reaching its nadir and especially threatening beleaguered minorities in aggressively majoritarian contexts, and peacefully praying for sanity in society. Meanwhile, a finely crafted essay is also prepared for publication, once every two years, if not earlier, its contents perhaps reminding readers of how episodes of violence perpetrated by a few individuals or even sacred figures often lead to terrible consequences for everyone around them.

Unemployed for ten years after completing his PhD, Professor Curley spent the next twenty years offering his distinguished services to the Department of Liberal Studies at Western Washington University, Bellingham, United States of America, starting as a lecturer in 1991 and retiring as a professor in 2012. He continues to be associated with the university as Emeritus Professor. Many friends in West Bengal and Bangladesh continue to look forward to his visits for research in local archives and guest lectures at their institutions. It was at one such event at the prestigious Centre for Studies in Social Sciences, Calcutta, that this writer first met Professor Curley so very fortuitously. He is among the few senior scholars who seriously read and offer comments on the works of younger researchers, sharing ideas completely selflessly. Mostly, new work is treated with cynical rejection or resounding silence. 
Behula sails with the body of her deceased husband, Lakhindar, in a scene from Manasamangal.

The Mangalkavya texts include versions of the famous Chandimangal, especially that of Mukunda Chakrabarti, Shitalamangal by Krishnaram Das and Annadamangal by Bharatchandra Ray, besides the equally famous texts such as Dharmamangal by Ghanaram Chakrabarty and Tirthamangal by Bijayram Sen. For Professor Curley, though religious and didactic in content, the texts also offer windows into worldly concerns, such as political, economic, social and patriarchal difficulties, the resolution of which required divine intervention. The powers of the deities were to be invoked in public, as the texts were composed for performance before an audience, not to be read in solitude. Modern historians can thus usefully explore the texts both for their contents and the contexts of their production. This can also help us understand changes in genre and narrative for a better appreciation of how they shifted the balance between didactic and ritual purposes on the one hand and performative pleasures – erotic, comic or defiant – on the other.
 
An aerial view of Behular Basor Ghor in Gokul, Bogura, an archaeological site containing the remains of an early Buddhist temple. Local tradition associates the site with Behula and Lakhindar, whose story is celebrated in Bengali Manasamangal literature. Photo: Mostafa Shabuj

Professor Curley has argued for a sustained reading of these narratives to gain a better historical understanding of the contexts in which they were composed and performed. According to him, ‘A good historian should be a good reader of the texts of Mangalkavya, and someone who can imagine performative possibilities of texts which mostly are no longer performed’. The common purpose of the genre was to benefit authors, performers and audiences, because performances were intended to act upon and bring about some good (mangal) for all. For this idea of the general public good to prevail, the texts sometimes also called for defiance of those in authority. As the all-powerful goddesses proclaimed: mian-bibi raaji, tow ki korbe kaaji!

Raziuddin Aquil is Professor of History at the University of Delhi, India.

item.title: The Daily Star – The Shenzhen gambit: Trump, Xi, Putin, and the unsettled global order
item.description:
“The old is dying and the new cannot be born.”

— Antonio Gramsci

Donald Trump's forthcoming meeting with Xi Jinping and Vladimir Putin in Shenzhen is unprecedented in its geopolitical symbolism, although its capacity to produce substantive agreements remains uncertain. Scheduled for November 19 on the margins of the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) summit, the encounter brings together the leaders of three nuclear powers whose interests overlap but whose strategic ambitions differ profoundly. Nuclear arms control and the conflict involving Iran are expected to feature in their discussions. Trump has also indicated that he intends to raise Ukraine, although American officials had initially suggested that the war would not form part of the trilateral agenda. The encounter comes at a consequential moment for all three leaders. Trump arrives in China following a Democratic electoral resurgence that has weakened his domestic political position, while the controversy surrounding NVIDIA has exposed vulnerabilities in America's technological pre-eminence and its increasingly contentious policy toward China.

But Shenzhen is more than a stage for three leaders seeking diplomatic advantage. It offers a vantage point from which to examine a deeper transformation: the shifting centre of gravity of the international system under the weight of strategic asymmetries. The contest is no longer simply between established and emerging powers, or between competing visions of a multipolar world. It concerns who can shape the economic, technological, military, and institutional foundations of the emerging order—and whether any single power can still command international authority.

The setting is revealing. Shenzhen, emblematic of China's industrial and technological ascent, provides the backdrop for a meeting taking place alongside a regional economic summit but addressing questions of global consequence. The contest for the centre is unfolding on the margins of APEC, even as the meaning of geopolitical centrality itself changes.

Presidential compensation and the calculations of power

The November 3 midterm elections have fundamentally altered the political landscape in Washington. Democratic victories, including the party's capture of both chambers of Congress, represent a substantial repudiation of the Trump administration's domestic record. The electoral reversal ends the Republican congressional trifecta and promises intensified legislative scrutiny, investigations, budgetary constraints, and resistance to the administration's policy ambitions.

The expression "Blue Tsunami" captures the scale of the Democratic resurgence, but its implications extend beyond the redistribution of congressional seats. It signals an erosion of Trump's political mandate and raises questions about the durability of his governing coalition. Although he retains the constitutional authority of the presidency, the electoral verdict has changed the institutional conditions under which that authority can be exercised. Political power depends not only on constitutional entitlement but also on public confidence, legislative support, and the capacity to translate political ambition into governing outcomes.

Trump's journey to China offers an opportunity to counter this domestic predicament through international visibility. A president whose political standing has diminished can seek to recover prestige by presenting himself as the indispensable interlocutor of the world's most powerful states. The Shenzhen meeting thus becomes an exercise in presidential compensation: an attempt to offset the loss of domestic political momentum through the performance of consequential statesmanship. Yet diplomatic visibility should not be confused with achievement. A photograph of three leaders together is neither a strategic settlement nor a reversal of an electoral verdict at home.

Xi Jinping has a different incentive. The presence of the American and Russian presidents on Chinese soil reinforces Beijing's claim to a central place in global diplomacy. China can present itself not merely as a regional power or economic competitor but as an indispensable participant in managing international security. Yet its advocacy of multilateralism and an inclusive international order sits uneasily alongside a gathering in which three powerful states may discuss questions affecting countries beyond their immediate circle.

For Vladimir Putin, the meeting offers recognition at a time when Russia's invasion of Ukraine has brought it into sustained confrontation with much of the Western world. A public encounter with the American and Chinese presidents allows him to present Russia as an indispensable participant in international security rather than a power that can be isolated or disregarded.

Their calculations may converge, but their strategic objectives do not. Washington seeks to preserve its pre-eminence while managing the costs of confrontation. Beijing seeks recognition of its growing influence and greater room to shape international arrangements. Moscow seeks validation of its great-power status and relief from diplomatic marginalisation. Their encounter may produce temporary accommodation without establishing a shared vision of international order.
The Republican Party’s loss of control of both chambers of Congress marks a major electoral setback for US President Donald Trump, potentially reshaping the balance of power in Washington. Photo: Umit Bektas/Reuters

The shifting centre and the weight of asymmetry

The traditional centre of the international system has rested on American economic, financial, military, and institutional predominance. That position has not disappeared. The United States retains formidable advantages: the dollar's international role, its global alliance networks, its technological ecosystem, its research institutions, and its military reach. These advantages are embedded in institutions and infrastructures that cannot be displaced simply by the rise of a competitor. Yet the capacity to exercise them without encountering consequential resistance has diminished.

China has altered the equation. Its manufacturing depth, industrial capacity, expanding technological capabilities, and extensive economic relationships provide forms of leverage that cannot be measured by military strength alone. Its position in global production networks gives it influence over supply chains and markets on which other economies depend. In the Indo-Pacific, trade, infrastructure, technology, and security have become increasingly difficult to disentangle.

Russia occupies a different position. Its economic weight is considerably narrower than that of the United States or China, but its nuclear arsenal, energy resources, military capabilities, and capacity to disrupt existing arrangements give it geopolitical influence disproportionate to its economic size. Russia cannot reproduce China's industrial reach or America's financial and institutional influence. It can, however, impose costs and complicate the strategic calculations of both.

This is the significance of strategic asymmetry. The three powers do not possess equivalent resources or exercise influence through comparable mechanisms. American financial networks and alliances, Chinese industrial and technological capacity, and Russian military and geopolitical instruments of disruption represent different configurations of power. Their capabilities overlap without becoming interchangeable.

The emerging international order therefore cannot be adequately described as a conventional multipolar system in which several powers occupy roughly equivalent positions. Nor is it simply a transition from American to Chinese hegemony. It is a more complicated configuration in which different forms of power are distributed unevenly, creating dependencies, vulnerabilities, and opportunities for leverage. A country may dominate one domain while remaining exposed in another.

The centre is consequently not moving in a straightforward line from Washington to Beijing. It is becoming more contested and distributed across domains. The capacity to shape the international system increasingly depends on controlling critical technological infrastructures, securing supply chains, influencing regional institutions, and managing economic dependencies, as well as on military superiority. Shenzhen embodies this transformation: a city once peripheral to the global economy has become central to China's industrial and technological integration, while the institutional setting of the trilateral encounter remains marginal to the wider international community it may affect. Material power is changing faster than the institutions through which it is collectively governed.

Nuclear arms control and the limits of trilateral diplomacy

Nuclear arms control is among the most consequential subjects expected to arise in Shenzhen. The expiration of the New START treaty on February 5, 2026, removed the last remaining treaty-based restrictions on the strategic nuclear arsenals of the United States and Russia. Although Putin had offered to continue observing the treaty's central numerical limits for another year, that proposal did not renew the treaty or establish a binding successor arrangement.

Trump's interest in a new framework that includes China reflects a changed strategic landscape. China's nuclear arsenal is expanding, and its capabilities cannot be excluded indefinitely from discussions about nuclear stability. Yet a trilateral framework confronts a fundamental asymmetry. The American and Russian arsenals remain substantially larger than China's, giving Beijing little incentive to accept numerical restrictions that could constrain its ability to approach the capabilities of the established nuclear powers.

From China's perspective, equal obligations imposed on states with unequal starting positions could institutionalise a strategic disadvantage. Washington, by contrast, has an interest in preventing China's nuclear expansion from proceeding without transparency or restraint. Moscow may also see advantages in bringing China into negotiations while remaining wary of arrangements that limit its own strategic flexibility.
British Prime Minister Winston Churchill, US President Franklin D. Roosevelt and Soviet leader Joseph Stalin at the Yalta Conference in February 1945. Their negotiations helped shape the postwar international order, illustrating the enduring influence of great-power diplomacy on smaller nations. Photo: Wikimedia Commons

Arms control requires verification, transparency, reciprocal obligations, and institutional continuity. These conditions are difficult to establish even between adversaries with a long history of negotiated restraint. They are harder still when the participants differ so substantially in the scale and composition of their arsenals. The meeting may therefore be significant less for an immediate settlement than for acknowledging that nuclear stability can no longer be addressed exclusively through the traditional Washington-Moscow relationship. Including China, however, cannot mean simply extending an old framework to a third participant. A durable arrangement must recognise different strategic circumstances while establishing credible limits and reciprocal obligations.

Iran, Ukraine, and the politics of exclusion

The conflicts involving Iran and Ukraine raise a related question: whether great-power diplomacy can manage international crises without subordinating the political agency of the states directly affected. Washington may hope that Beijing and Moscow can help restrain Tehran or contribute to a diplomatic resolution. Both countries maintain important relationships with Iran, although neither necessarily shares the American administration's objectives. China has economic and strategic interests in regional stability and in maintaining its relationship with Tehran. Russia has cultivated military and diplomatic ties with Iran as its confrontation with the West has deepened.

Their influence may be useful in preventing escalation, but cooperation cannot be assumed. China and Russia have reasons to discourage a conflict that threatens regional stability; they also have reasons to resist an American initiative that strengthens Washington's position in the region. Their willingness to exert influence will depend on whether the proposed outcome serves their own strategic interests. Their ability to influence Tehran does not give them the right to determine Iran's political future.

Ukraine makes the problem of exclusion more visible. Although US officials had initially indicated that the war would not form part of the trilateral meeting's agenda, Trump subsequently said he intended to raise it with Xi and Putin. The uncertainty surrounding Ukraine's place in the discussions is itself revealing. The possibility of negotiating the future of a sovereign country among three powerful states raises questions about whose interests are represented and whose political agency risks being subordinated to great-power calculations.

This is not an argument against direct negotiations among major powers. Such negotiations may be indispensable to reducing the risk of escalation, particularly when nuclear-armed states are involved. But crisis management and political legitimacy are not interchangeable. An agreement that excludes those whose sovereignty, security, and territory are at stake may produce a temporary accommodation without establishing a durable peace. The principle extends beyond Ukraine and Iran: states across the Middle East and the Indo-Pacific have interests that cannot be reduced to the preferences of Washington, Beijing, or Moscow.

NVIDIA and the vulnerability of technological power

The political significance of Shenzhen cannot be fully understood without considering the turmoil surrounding NVIDIA, one of the most consequential corporations in the global artificial-intelligence economy. Jensen Huang's resignation as chief executive, announced on November 12, followed reports concerning personal relationships and an alleged foreign-intelligence effort involving a woman whom US intelligence reportedly suspects of having connections to Chinese espionage.

The allegations require careful qualification. NVIDIA's board announced an independent investigation into whether Huang had been targeted by a foreign-intelligence operation while maintaining that it had no reason to believe national-security information or company secrets had been compromised. His resignation establishes neither that espionage occurred nor that classified information was obtained. Until the investigation establishes what happened, the allegations must remain distinct from proven findings.

The significance of the episode extends beyond the circumstances of one executive's departure. NVIDIA occupies a pivotal position in the global AI economy, supplying advanced processors and computing platforms essential to the development of increasingly sophisticated artificial-intelligence systems. Its commercial interests have also placed it at the centre of a strategic dispute in Washington: whether American technological leadership is best preserved by restricting China's access to advanced semiconductors or by maintaining commercial engagement and the markets that sustain American innovation.

Huang had been an influential advocate of retaining access to China, arguing that technological leadership depends not simply on restricting competitors but also on preserving market reach, commercial incentives, and the resources generated by global competition. His departure removes a prominent corporate voice from an already contentious policy debate. It would nevertheless be premature to suggest that it has itself reset American semiconductor policy.
Nvidia chief executive Jensen Huang's resignation on 12 November 2026, amid allegations involving a suspected Chinese intelligence operative, has raised concerns about the company's future and US–China technology relations. Photo: Reuters

Advanced semiconductors have become instruments of economic power, military modernisation, industrial competitiveness, and technological sovereignty. Washington's export controls can constrain China's access to advanced chips, but they also risk accelerating Beijing's pursuit of technological self-sufficiency and fragmenting the global markets on which American firms depend. Unrestricted access, conversely, may facilitate the transfer of technologies with direct military and strategic applications. Measures intended to preserve American technological superiority may thus accelerate the development of alternatives capable of challenging it.

Washington's leverage also has a significant counterweight. China's dominance in the processing and refining of rare earth elements and other critical minerals gives Beijing its own capacity to exploit strategic supply-chain dependencies. Restrictions on their export can expose vulnerabilities across American and allied industries, from advanced electronics and electric vehicles to renewable energy and defence production. Washington can restrict China's access to advanced chips, while Beijing can constrain the supply of materials essential to important segments of the industrial and technological infrastructure on which American power depends.

This is not simply a contest between national security and corporate interests. It concerns control over the infrastructures, markets, and material dependencies that sustain technological power. American leadership in chip design and AI infrastructure rests on globally distributed production networks, specialised manufacturing, international markets, and private corporations whose commercial calculations do not necessarily coincide with government priorities. China's leverage over critical-mineral processing exposes a corresponding vulnerability in the American and allied industrial ecosystem. Technological pre-eminence does not automatically translate into strategic autonomy.

The NVIDIA episode therefore illuminates a structural contest that presidential accommodation alone cannot resolve. The technological relationship between Washington and Beijing is shaped by industrial capacity, access to markets, critical resources, and the global networks on which both economies depend. A summit may create room for negotiation or moderate immediate tensions, but it cannot eliminate these underlying dependencies.

The return of great-power politics?

The Shenzhen meeting invites comparisons with earlier moments when powerful states attempted to manage international disorder through direct negotiation. The Concert of Europe, established after the Napoleonic Wars, rested on the premise that the principal powers could preserve stability through consultation and recognition of their shared interests. Its significance lay in establishing practices of crisis management and restraint. Yet it was neither a democratic institution nor an impartial guarantor of peace. Its stability depended partly on suppressing revolutionary movements and preserving a conservative European balance of power.

The Yalta Conference in 1945 represented a different configuration. The victorious Allied powers contemplated the postwar settlement and the institutional architecture of a new international order. Its consequences for Eastern Europe demonstrated the dangers of great-power bargaining when the political future of smaller states becomes subordinate to the strategic calculations of dominant powers. The analogy is not that Shenzhen will reproduce Yalta, but that both episodes invite scrutiny of who participates in decisions and who bears their consequences.

Neither precedent offers a direct template for the present. The international system is more complex, economic interdependence is deeper, and technological competition has created forms of strategic vulnerability earlier generations could scarcely have imagined. Yet both examples illuminate a recurring feature of international politics: when established institutions appear inadequate to manage conflict, powerful states turn to direct bargaining among themselves.

The appeal of a trilateral summit lies in the possibility that the leaders of three consequential nuclear powers can establish understandings that reduce the risk of miscalculation. But a concert of powers requires more than the ability to convene. It requires shared purpose, institutional continuity, and a willingness to accept limits on unilateral action. Unlike the Concert of Europe, which rested on an exclusionary but recognisable commitment to preserving a continental balance, or Yalta, which was embedded in the Allied wartime settlement and the emerging United Nations framework, the three powers meeting in Shenzhen have no common institutional principles or agreed conception of international order to sustain their cooperation.

Their differences concern the very terms on which international authority should be exercised: the meaning of sovereignty, the legitimacy of intervention, the role of economic coercion, and the authority of international institutions. Direct bargaining may sometimes be more effective than cumbersome multilateral negotiations, particularly when the immediate objective is to prevent escalation. But an agreement among powerful states cannot by itself provide the institutional foundations of a stable or inclusive order. Europe, Japan, India, Southeast Asian countries, and states across the Middle East have interests that cannot be reduced to the preferences of Washington, Beijing, and Moscow.
Diplomats gather at the Congress of Paris in 1856, where major European powers negotiated the settlement of the Crimean War. The gathering illustrates how great-power diplomacy has historically shaped international order and the political fortunes of smaller states. Painting: Édouard Dubufe.

Shenzhen and the uncertain foundations of a new equilibrium

The meeting in Shenzhen may produce no binding agreement, perhaps little more than a statement of intentions and a commitment to continue discussions. That would not diminish its diplomatic significance. At a time when established mechanisms of international cooperation are under strain, the willingness of three consequential powers to engage directly carries weight in its own right. The more consequential question is whether their encounter can establish a basis for managing the conflicts and dependencies that bring them together.

For Xi, the meeting offers an opportunity to consolidate China's recognition as an indispensable participant in shaping global affairs. For Putin, it demonstrates that Russia retains strategic relevance that Washington and Beijing cannot disregard. For Trump, it provides an occasion to project international leadership despite a damaging electoral setback at home. Their interests may overlap sufficiently to produce an understanding, but they do not constitute a shared vision of international order.

The deeper issue is how international authority will be constituted when its principal sources no longer converge within a single geopolitical centre. Economic capacity, technological infrastructure, military deterrence, and institutional influence are distributed unevenly. These asymmetries create opportunities for leverage but also generate dependencies. A state may enjoy decisive advantages in one domain while remaining vulnerable in another; it may obstruct an existing arrangement without possessing the resources or international confidence to replace it. The resulting instability reflects not simply a redistribution of power, but the absence of an accepted framework for reconciling its competing expressions.

Trump's journey to China illustrates this predicament. His effort to project global leadership reflects the political incentives of a president whose domestic authority has weakened. Yet American influence rests on more than presidential initiative or military and economic preponderance. Its credibility depends on institutional continuity, dependable alliances, and the capacity of successive administrations to sustain negotiated commitments. Personal diplomacy can open channels of communication, but cannot independently provide the continuity and mutual confidence required for durable settlements.

The three leaders may find grounds for accommodation in Shenzhen without resolving the contradictions that make it necessary. Their meeting could reduce immediate tensions, clarify strategic intentions, or establish channels for further negotiation. Such achievements would matter. “The old is dying and the new cannot be born.”

— Antonio Gramsci

Donald Trump's forthcoming meeting with Xi Jinping and Vladimir Putin in Shenzhen is unprecedented in its geopolitical symbolism, although its capacity to produce substantive agreements remains uncertain. Scheduled for November 19 on the margins of the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) summit, the encounter brings together the leaders of three nuclear powers whose interests overlap but whose strategic ambitions differ profoundly. Nuclear arms control and the conflict involving Iran are expected to feature in their discussions. Trump has also indicated that he intends to raise Ukraine, although American officials had initially suggested that the war would not form part of the trilateral agenda. The encounter comes at a consequential moment for all three leaders. Trump arrives in China following a Democratic electoral resurgence that has weakened his domestic political position, while the controversy surrounding NVIDIA has exposed vulnerabilities in America's technological pre-eminence and its increasingly contentious policy toward China.

But Shenzhen is more than a stage for three leaders seeking diplomatic advantage. It offers a vantage point from which to examine a deeper transformation: the shifting centre of gravity of the international system under the weight of strategic asymmetries. The contest is no longer simply between established and emerging powers, or between competing visions of a multipolar world. It concerns who can shape the economic, technological, military, and institutional foundations of the emerging order—and whether any single power can still command international authority.

The setting is revealing. Shenzhen, emblematic of China's industrial and technological ascent, provides the backdrop for a meeting taking place alongside a regional economic summit but addressing questions of global consequence. The contest for the centre is unfolding on the margins of APEC, even as the meaning of geopolitical centrality itself changes.

Presidential compensation and the calculations of power

The November 3 midterm elections have fundamentally altered the political landscape in Washington. Democratic victories, including the party's capture of both chambers of Congress, represent a substantial repudiation of the Trump administration's domestic record. The electoral reversal ends the Republican congressional trifecta and promises intensified legislative scrutiny, investigations, budgetary constraints, and resistance to the administration's policy ambitions.

The expression "Blue Tsunami" captures the scale of the Democratic resurgence, but its implications extend beyond the redistribution of congressional seats. It signals an erosion of Trump's political mandate and raises questions about the durability of his governing coalition. Although he retains the constitutional authority of the presidency, the electoral verdict has changed the institutional conditions under which that authority can be exercised. Political power depends not only on constitutional entitlement but also on public confidence, legislative support, and the capacity to translate political ambition into governing outcomes.

Trump's journey to China offers an opportunity to counter this domestic predicament through international visibility. A president whose political standing has diminished can seek to recover prestige by presenting himself as the indispensable interlocutor of the world's most powerful states. The Shenzhen meeting thus becomes an exercise in presidential compensation: an attempt to offset the loss of domestic political momentum through the performance of consequential statesmanship. Yet diplomatic visibility should not be confused with achievement. A photograph of three leaders together is neither a strategic settlement nor a reversal of an electoral verdict at home.

Xi Jinping has a different incentive. The presence of the American and Russian presidents on Chinese soil reinforces Beijing's claim to a central place in global diplomacy. China can present itself not merely as a regional power or economic competitor but as an indispensable participant in managing international security. Yet its advocacy of multilateralism and an inclusive international order sits uneasily alongside a gathering in which three powerful states may discuss questions affecting countries beyond their immediate circle.

For Vladimir Putin, the meeting offers recognition at a time when Russia's invasion of Ukraine has brought it into sustained confrontation with much of the Western world. A public encounter with the American and Chinese presidents allows him to present Russia as an indispensable participant in international security rather than a power that can be isolated or disregarded.

Their calculations may converge, but their strategic objectives do not. Washington seeks to preserve its pre-eminence while managing the costs of confrontation. Beijing seeks recognition of its growing influence and greater room to shape international arrangements. Moscow seeks validation of its great-power status and relief from diplomatic marginalisation. Their encounter may produce temporary accommodation without establishing a shared vision of international order.
The Republican Party’s loss of control of both chambers of Congress marks a major electoral setback for US President Donald Trump, potentially reshaping the balance of power in Washington. Photo: Umit Bektas/Reuters

The shifting centre and the weight of asymmetry

The traditional centre of the international system has rested on American economic, financial, military, and institutional predominance. That position has not disappeared. The United States retains formidable advantages: the dollar's international role, its global alliance networks, its technological ecosystem, its research institutions, and its military reach. These advantages are embedded in institutions and infrastructures that cannot be displaced simply by the rise of a competitor. Yet the capacity to exercise them without encountering consequential resistance has diminished.

China has altered the equation. Its manufacturing depth, industrial capacity, expanding technological capabilities, and extensive economic relationships provide forms of leverage that cannot be measured by military strength alone. Its position in global production networks gives it influence over supply chains and markets on which other economies depend. In the Indo-Pacific, trade, infrastructure, technology, and security have become increasingly difficult to disentangle.

Russia occupies a different position. Its economic weight is considerably narrower than that of the United States or China, but its nuclear arsenal, energy resources, military capabilities, and capacity to disrupt existing arrangements give it geopolitical influence disproportionate to its economic size. Russia cannot reproduce China's industrial reach or America's financial and institutional influence. It can, however, impose costs and complicate the strategic calculations of both.

This is the significance of strategic asymmetry. The three powers do not possess equivalent resources or exercise influence through comparable mechanisms. American financial networks and alliances, Chinese industrial and technological capacity, and Russian military and geopolitical instruments of disruption represent different configurations of power. Their capabilities overlap without becoming interchangeable.

The emerging international order therefore cannot be adequately described as a conventional multipolar system in which several powers occupy roughly equivalent positions. Nor is it simply a transition from American to Chinese hegemony. It is a more complicated configuration in which different forms of power are distributed unevenly, creating dependencies, vulnerabilities, and opportunities for leverage. A country may dominate one domain while remaining exposed in another.

The centre is consequently not moving in a straightforward line from Washington to Beijing. It is becoming more contested and distributed across domains. The capacity to shape the international system increasingly depends on controlling critical technological infrastructures, securing supply chains, influencing regional institutions, and managing economic dependencies, as well as on military superiority. Shenzhen embodies this transformation: a city once peripheral to the global economy has become central to China's industrial and technological integration, while the institutional setting of the trilateral encounter remains marginal to the wider international community it may affect. Material power is changing faster than the institutions through which it is collectively governed.

Nuclear arms control and the limits of trilateral diplomacy

Nuclear arms control is among the most consequential subjects expected to arise in Shenzhen. The expiration of the New START treaty on February 5, 2026, removed the last remaining treaty-based restrictions on the strategic nuclear arsenals of the United States and Russia. Although Putin had offered to continue observing the treaty's central numerical limits for another year, that proposal did not renew the treaty or establish a binding successor arrangement.

Trump's interest in a new framework that includes China reflects a changed strategic landscape. China's nuclear arsenal is expanding, and its capabilities cannot be excluded indefinitely from discussions about nuclear stability. Yet a trilateral framework confronts a fundamental asymmetry. The American and Russian arsenals remain substantially larger than China's, giving Beijing little incentive to accept numerical restrictions that could constrain its ability to approach the capabilities of the established nuclear powers.

From China's perspective, equal obligations imposed on states with unequal starting positions could institutionalise a strategic disadvantage. Washington, by contrast, has an interest in preventing China's nuclear expansion from proceeding without transparency or restraint. Moscow may also see advantages in bringing China into negotiations while remaining wary of arrangements that limit its own strategic flexibility.
British Prime Minister Winston Churchill, US President Franklin D. Roosevelt and Soviet leader Joseph Stalin at the Yalta Conference in February 1945. Their negotiations helped shape the postwar international order, illustrating the enduring influence of great-power diplomacy on smaller nations. Photo: Wikimedia Commons

Arms control requires verification, transparency, reciprocal obligations, and institutional continuity. These conditions are difficult to establish even between adversaries with a long history of negotiated restraint. They are harder still when the participants differ so substantially in the scale and composition of their arsenals. The meeting may therefore be significant less for an immediate settlement than for acknowledging that nuclear stability can no longer be addressed exclusively through the traditional Washington-Moscow relationship. Including China, however, cannot mean simply extending an old framework to a third participant. A durable arrangement must recognise different strategic circumstances while establishing credible limits and reciprocal obligations.

Iran, Ukraine, and the politics of exclusion

The conflicts involving Iran and Ukraine raise a related question: whether great-power diplomacy can manage international crises without subordinating the political agency of the states directly affected. Washington may hope that Beijing and Moscow can help restrain Tehran or contribute to a diplomatic resolution. Both countries maintain important relationships with Iran, although neither necessarily shares the American administration's objectives. China has economic and strategic interests in regional stability and in maintaining its relationship with Tehran. Russia has cultivated military and diplomatic ties with Iran as its confrontation with the West has deepened.

Their influence may be useful in preventing escalation, but cooperation cannot be assumed. China and Russia have reasons to discourage a conflict that threatens regional stability; they also have reasons to resist an American initiative that strengthens Washington's position in the region. Their willingness to exert influence will depend on whether the proposed outcome serves their own strategic interests. Their ability to influence Tehran does not give them the right to determine Iran's political future.

Ukraine makes the problem of exclusion more visible. The uncertainty surrounding Ukraine's place in the discussions is itself revealing. The possibility of negotiating the future of a sovereign country among three powerful states raises questions about whose interests are represented and whose political agency risks being subordinated to great-power calculations.

This is not an argument against direct negotiations among major powers. Such negotiations may be indispensable to reducing the risk of escalation, particularly when nuclear-armed states are involved. But crisis management and political legitimacy are not interchangeable. An agreement that excludes those whose sovereignty, security, and territory are at stake may produce a temporary accommodation without establishing a durable peace. The principle extends beyond Ukraine and Iran: states across the Middle East and the Indo-Pacific have interests that cannot be reduced to the preferences of Washington, Beijing, or Moscow.

NVIDIA and the vulnerability of technological power

The political significance of Shenzhen cannot be fully understood without considering the turmoil surrounding NVIDIA, one of the most consequential corporations in the global artificial-intelligence economy. Jensen Huang's resignation as chief executive, announced on November 12, followed reports concerning personal relationships and an alleged foreign-intelligence effort involving a woman whom US intelligence reportedly suspects of having connections to Chinese espionage.

The allegations require careful qualification. NVIDIA's board announced an independent investigation into whether Huang had been targeted by a foreign-intelligence operation while maintaining that it had no reason to believe national-security information or company secrets had been compromised. His resignation establishes neither that espionage occurred nor that classified information was obtained. Until the investigation establishes what happened, the allegations must remain distinct from proven findings.

The significance of the episode extends beyond the circumstances of one executive's departure. NVIDIA occupies a pivotal position in the global AI economy, supplying advanced processors and computing platforms essential to the development of increasingly sophisticated artificial-intelligence systems. Its commercial interests have also placed it at the centre of a strategic dispute in Washington: whether American technological leadership is best preserved by restricting China's access to advanced semiconductors or by maintaining commercial engagement and the markets that sustain American innovation.

Huang had been an influential advocate of retaining access to China, arguing that technological leadership depends not simply on restricting competitors but also on preserving market reach, commercial incentives, and the resources generated by global competition. His departure removes a prominent corporate voice from an already contentious policy debate. It would nevertheless be premature to suggest that it has itself reset American semiconductor policy.

Advanced semiconductors have become instruments of economic power, military modernisation, industrial competitiveness, and technological sovereignty. Washington's export controls can constrain China's access to advanced chips, but they also risk accelerating Beijing's pursuit of technological self-sufficiency and fragmenting the global markets on which American firms depend. Unrestricted access, conversely, may facilitate the transfer of technologies with direct military and strategic applications. Measures intended to preserve American technological superiority may thus accelerate the development of alternatives capable of challenging it.

Washington's leverage also has a significant counterweight. China's dominance in the processing and refining of rare earth elements and other critical minerals gives Beijing its own capacity to exploit strategic supply-chain dependencies. Restrictions on their export can expose vulnerabilities across American and allied industries, from advanced electronics and electric vehicles to renewable energy and defence production. Washington can restrict China's access to advanced chips, while Beijing can constrain the supply of materials essential to important segments of the industrial and technological infrastructure on which American power depends.

This is not simply a contest between national security and corporate interests. It concerns control over the infrastructures, markets, and material dependencies that sustain technological power. American leadership in chip design and AI infrastructure rests on globally distributed production networks, specialised manufacturing, international markets, and private corporations whose commercial calculations do not necessarily coincide with government priorities. China's leverage over critical-mineral processing exposes a corresponding vulnerability in the American and allied industrial ecosystem. Technological pre-eminence does not automatically translate into strategic autonomy.

The NVIDIA episode therefore illuminates a structural contest that presidential accommodation alone cannot resolve. The technological relationship between Washington and Beijing is shaped by industrial capacity, access to markets, critical resources, and the global networks on which both economies depend. A summit may create room for negotiation or moderate immediate tensions, but it cannot eliminate these underlying dependencies.

The return of great-power politics?

The Shenzhen meeting invites comparisons with earlier moments when powerful states attempted to manage international disorder through direct negotiation. The Concert of Europe, established after the Napoleonic Wars, rested on the premise that the principal powers could preserve stability through consultation and recognition of their shared interests. Its stability depended partly on suppressing revolutionary movements and preserving a conservative European balance of power.

item.title: The Daily Star – Can Bangladesh become a regional pharmaceutical powerhouse?
item.description:
Chinese biotech companies are supplying an increasing share of the world's experimental medicines. Their rise could help emerging pharmaceutical economies move beyond generic manufacturing.

Roche's recent agreement with China's Rona Therapeutics would have attracted attention on the strength of its numbers alone: $100 million upfront and another $1.06 billion in potential milestone payments for an experimental obesity treatment. What makes the deal more interesting is where the science originated.

A decade ago, Western pharmaceutical companies went to China largely for inexpensive active ingredients, contract manufacturing and increasingly sophisticated research services. Today, they are buying molecules discovered and developed by Chinese companies.

According to Reuters, Chinese drugmakers have announced international licensing agreements with a combined potential value exceeding $139 billion so far in 2026. Most of that money is contingent on clinical and commercial milestones, many of which may never be reached. Even so, the volume of transactions shows that China has become a substantial source of new drug candidates for an industry facing mounting patent expirations and increasingly expensive development programmes.
Researchers work at a WuXi AppTec laboratory in Shanghai, China, on 25 April 2016. Once known for supplying inexpensive pharmaceutical ingredients and manufacturing services, China has emerged as a major source of innovative drug candidates, creating new licensing opportunities for countries such as Bangladesh. Photo: Reuters/Aly Song

The question now extends beyond who discovers the next generation of medicines. It concerns who will develop, register and sell them in the many countries that fall outside the commercial priorities of multinational drugmakers.

Pharmaceutical innovation has always had a geographical asymmetry. Discovery and clinical development costs are global, but the greatest financial returns are concentrated in a handful of wealthy markets. Companies naturally prioritise the United States, Europe and Japan, where reimbursement systems and purchasing power can support the prices of innovative treatments. Elsewhere, access is often delayed, sometimes indefinitely.

The arrival of Chinese innovators in global licensing offers a possible way to change that equation.

Drug rights need not be sold as a single worldwide package. They can be divided by territory, allowing an originator to retain some markets, license others to major pharmaceutical companies and work with regional partners where a dedicated commercial operation would make little economic sense.

India's Dr Reddy's Laboratories is an instructive example. In 2023, it secured rights to Shanghai Junshi Biosciences' cancer immunotherapy toripalimab across 21 countries, including India, Brazil and South Africa, under an agreement worth up to $728 million. The company subsequently introduced the treatment in India.

Dr Reddy's did not invent toripalimab. Its commercial contribution was to acquire the relevant rights and undertake the work needed to bring the medicine to patients in its licensed markets. That required regulatory expertise, capital, market knowledge and an understanding of the clinical evidence. These capabilities have substantial economic value, even when the original discovery takes place elsewhere.

There are limits to the model. Many Chinese companies prefer to license worldwide rights to a single multinational partner. Others retain territories for their own commercial operations. Regional opportunities arise only where rights remain available, and a prospective partner can offer something the originator cannot efficiently accomplish itself.

For pharmaceutical industries built around manufacturing generic medicines, however, the possibility deserves serious attention.
Customers purchase medicines at a pharmacy in Bangladesh. Patent exemptions have enabled domestic manufacturers to produce affordable versions of medicines that remain patent-protected elsewhere. Photo: Habibur Rahman

Consider Bangladesh. Its pharmaceutical industry supplies roughly 98 per cent of domestic medicine demand and exports to more than 160 countries. Companies including Beximco, Eskayef, Incepta and Renata have developed manufacturing capabilities that compare favourably with those of much larger economies. It is an unusual industrial achievement for a country at Bangladesh's income level.

Much of that success rests on a particular legal advantage. As a least-developed country, Bangladesh has benefited from exemptions under World Trade Organization (WTO) rules that permit pharmaceutical production without enforcing certain patent obligations. Domestic manufacturers have used this freedom to make medicines that remain patent-protected elsewhere, often at a fraction of the original price.

The public health benefits are considerable. In 2026, Beximco began supplying a version of Vertex Pharmaceuticals' cystic fibrosis treatment at an annual adult price of approximately $12,750. The comparable branded therapy carries a US list price of roughly $370,000.

Yet the legal arrangement supporting this model will expire soon.

Bangladesh's transition has been deferred. On 29 October 2026, the United Nations General Assembly approved a three-year extension, moving the country's graduation from least-developed-country status to 24 November 2029. The decision is a welcome reprieve, but it gives Bangladesh only a finite window to prepare. Under WTO rules, the special pharmaceutical patent transition lasts until 2033 or until a country leaves the least-developed category, whichever comes first.

Graduation will not end generic manufacturing. Most established medicines eventually lose patent protection, and international trade rules provide safeguards for public health. But the commercial calculus for newer therapies will change. Bangladeshi companies seeking to manufacture and market patented medicines will increasingly have to negotiate with the rights holders.

That should prompt the industry to reconsider its business model.

The opportunity is to become a regional development and commercialisation partner for innovative medicines, including those originating in China. Bangladesh already has much of the necessary manufacturing infrastructure. It needs expertise to evaluate assets, negotiate licensing agreements, manage regulatory submissions and develop commercially viable markets.

Multinational pharmaceutical companies are familiar with these disciplines, which remain less developed in industries whose principal strength is generic production. Assessing a potential licence requires more than reviewing promising clinical results. A company must understand the mechanism of action, competing therapies, development risks, intellectual property, manufacturing requirements and the likely cost of bringing the medicine to market.

A candidate that appears attractive on the strength of early efficacy data can become a poor investment once the costs of additional trials, technology transfer, royalties and regulatory approval are included. Scientific discernment matters as much as negotiating skill.

Bangladesh would also face formidable competition. India has a far larger domestic market, experienced pharmaceutical business development teams and substantial expertise in clinical development. Chinese manufacturers, meanwhile, are moving further into finished medicines for export. Both have advantages that Bangladesh cannot easily replicate.

The sensible approach would therefore be selective. Rather than competing for expensive, high-profile assets, Bangladeshi companies could pursue approved products or late-stage candidates with credible clinical evidence and manageable development requirements. Regional rights covering several smaller markets in South Asia or Africa might be commercially attractive where individual national markets would not justify the investment.
As Bangladesh prepares for LDC graduation, its pharmaceutical industry's next challenge is to move beyond generic manufacturing by developing the scientific, regulatory and commercial expertise needed to secure licensing rights and bring innovative medicines to regional markets. Illustration: Mahiya Tabassum

Such agreements would need careful negotiation. A collection of small territories is not automatically a viable business. Differences in regulatory requirements, pricing, reimbursement and distribution can erode the apparent advantages of regional scale.

Regulation is a particularly pressing problem. Bangladesh's drug regulatory authority remains at level 2 on the World Health Organization's maturity scale, below the level 3 benchmark for a stable, well-functioning regulatory system. For companies aspiring to secure multinational licensing rights, stronger regulatory oversight is a commercial necessity. Licensors need confidence in manufacturing quality, pharmacovigilance, clinical data and the integrity of regulatory submissions.

Clinical research offers another route to differentiation. Bangladesh has a large patient population and established medical institutions, but attracting international trials requires reliable research infrastructure, trained investigators and consistent oversight. The ability to conduct well-managed studies in South Asian populations could give local companies a more credible role in the development of therapies intended for the region.

These are prosaic investments. They lack the visibility of a new pharmaceutical plant or a headline-grabbing licensing agreement. Yet they determine whether an industry can progress from producing medicines developed elsewhere to participating in their development and commercialisation.

The implications extend beyond Bangladesh.

Several emerging economies have spent decades pursuing pharmaceutical self-sufficiency through import substitution and generic manufacturing. Some have established successful domestic industries without acquiring the capabilities needed to evaluate innovative therapies or negotiate access to them. China's growing pipeline creates an opening for these countries to reconsider where they can compete.

They need not reproduce China's enormous research investment or attempt to discover every medicine themselves. But neither can they expect to succeed simply by offering inexpensive manufacturing. The more promising role is to become a capable commercial and development partner, able to identify worthwhile therapies, negotiate sensible terms and deliver them to markets that larger companies may otherwise neglect.
A worker operates equipment at a pharmaceutical manufacturing facility in Bangladesh. The country's pharmaceutical industry meets roughly 98 per cent of domestic medicine demand and exports to more than 160 countries, but faces new challenges as LDC graduation approaches. Photo: Rashed Shumon

There is a wider public health interest in getting this right. If Chinese innovation is absorbed primarily into the pipelines of Western pharmaceutical companies, the geography of drug discovery will have changed without necessarily improving access across much of the developing world. Regional licensing offers one possible remedy, although its success will depend on commercial incentives and competent institutions, not goodwill alone.

For Bangladesh, the choice is becoming immediate. Another three years of patent exemptions will provide useful time. It would also be easy to squander.

The country's pharmaceutical industry has already shown that it can manufacture sophisticated medicines at prices its population can afford. Its next test is whether it can acquire the scientific, regulatory and commercial expertise to negotiate access to medicines it did not invent.

That may prove harder than building the factories. It is also where the next stage of industrial growth is likely to be found.

Mukhtar Ahmed, PhD, is a drug developer, biotech executive and strategic adviser based in Palo Alto, California.

But the commercial calculus for newer therapies will change. Bangladeshi companies seeking to manufacture and market patented medicines will increasingly have to negotiate with the rights holders.

That should prompt the industry to reconsider its business model.

The opportunity is to become a regional development and commercialisation partner for innovative medicines, including those originating in China. Bangladesh already has much of the necessary manufacturing infrastructure. It needs expertise to evaluate assets, negotiate licensing agreements, manage regulatory submissions and develop commercially viable markets.

Multinational pharmaceutical companies are familiar with these disciplines, which remain less developed in industries whose principal strength is generic production. Assessing a potential licence requires more than reviewing promising clinical results. A company must understand the mechanism of action, competing therapies, development risks, intellectual property, manufacturing requirements and the likely cost of bringing the medicine to market.

A candidate that appears attractive on the strength of early efficacy data can become a poor investment once the costs of additional trials, technology transfer, royalties and regulatory approval are included. Scientific discernment matters as much as negotiating skill.

Bangladesh would also face formidable competition. India has a far larger domestic market, experienced pharmaceutical business development teams and substantial expertise in clinical development. Chinese manufacturers, meanwhile, are moving further into finished medicines for export. Both have advantages that Bangladesh cannot easily replicate.

The sensible approach would therefore be selective. Rather than competing for expensive, high-profile assets, Bangladeshi companies could pursue approved products or late-stage candidates with credible clinical evidence and manageable development requirements. Regional rights covering several smaller markets in South Asia or Africa might be commercially attractive where individual national markets would not justify the investment.
As Bangladesh prepares for LDC graduation, its pharmaceutical industry's next challenge is to move beyond generic manufacturing by developing the scientific, regulatory and commercial expertise needed to secure licensing rights and bring innovative medicines to regional markets. Illustration: Mahiya Tabassum

Such agreements would need careful negotiation. A collection of small territories is not automatically a viable business. Differences in regulatory requirements, pricing, reimbursement and distribution can erode the apparent advantages of regional scale.

Regulation is a particularly pressing problem. Bangladesh's drug regulatory authority remains at level 2 on the World Health Organization's maturity scale, below the level 3 benchmark for a stable, well-functioning regulatory system. For companies aspiring to secure multinational licensing rights, stronger regulatory oversight is a commercial necessity. Licensors need confidence in manufacturing quality, pharmacovigilance, clinical data and the integrity of regulatory submissions.

Clinical research offers another route to differentiation. Bangladesh has a large patient population and established medical institutions, but attracting international trials requires reliable research infrastructure, trained investigators and consistent oversight. The ability to conduct well-managed studies in South Asian populations could give local companies a more credible role in the development of therapies intended for the region.

These are prosaic investments. They lack the visibility of a new pharmaceutical plant or a headline-grabbing licensing agreement. Yet they determine whether an industry can progress from producing medicines developed elsewhere to participating in their development and commercialisation.

The implications extend beyond Bangladesh.

Several emerging economies have spent decades pursuing pharmaceutical self-sufficiency through import substitution and generic manufacturing. Some have established successful domestic industries without acquiring the capabilities needed to evaluate innovative therapies or negotiate access to them. China's growing pipeline creates an opening for these countries to reconsider where they can compete.

They need not reproduce China's enormous research investment or attempt to discover every medicine themselves. But neither can they expect to succeed simply by offering inexpensive manufacturing. The more promising role is to become a capable commercial and development partner, able to identify worthwhile therapies, negotiate sensible terms and deliver them to markets that larger companies may otherwise neglect.
A worker operates equipment at a pharmaceutical manufacturing facility in Bangladesh. The country's pharmaceutical industry meets roughly 98 per cent of domestic medicine demand and exports to more than 160 countries, but faces new challenges as LDC graduation approaches. Photo: Rashed Shumon

There is a wider public health interest in getting this right. If Chinese innovation is absorbed primarily into the pipelines of Western pharmaceutical companies, the geography of drug discovery will have changed without necessarily improving access across much of the developing world. Regional licensing offers one possible remedy, although its success will depend on commercial incentives and competent institutions, not goodwill alone.

For Bangladesh, the choice is becoming immediate. Another three years of patent exemptions will provide useful time. It would also be easy to squander.

The country's pharmaceutical industry has already shown that it can manufacture sophisticated medicines at prices its population can afford. Its next test is whether it can acquire the scientific, regulatory and commercial expertise to negotiate access to medicines it did not invent.

That may prove harder than building the factories. It is also where the next stage of industrial growth is likely to be found.

Mukhtar Ahmed, PhD, is a drug developer, biotech executive and strategic adviser based in Palo Alto, California.

item.title: The Daily Star – Bangladesh is building factories. Who will run their supply chains?
item.description:
Walk into the operations office of almost any large manufacturer in Bangladesh, including multinationals, and you will find a familiar pattern. The workers on the factory floor are Bangladeshi. The technicians keeping critical machines running are often from Sri Lanka. The managers planning production, sourcing inputs and moving goods are frequently from India, and so, typically, are the general managers. I have seen this first-hand at a US multinational operating here. After decades as one of the world's manufacturing nations, we still import the people who run our supply chains.

That gap is about to become far more expensive.

A bigger, harder industrial bet

Ready-made garments account for 80–83 per cent of our exports and employ some 4.4 million people. The country is now making a deliberate, capital-backed push into pharmaceuticals and active pharmaceutical ingredients (APIs), electronics, light engineering and technical textiles.
A worker operates pharmaceutical processing equipment at a facility in Tongi. As Bangladesh expands into pharmaceuticals and active pharmaceutical ingredients (APIs), the industry will need skilled professionals to manage complex supply chains, source regulated inputs from multiple countries and maintain international quality standards. Photo: Rashed Shumon

The numbers are not small. The National Special Economic Zone at Mirsharai–Sitakunda–Sonagazi, the Japanese Economic Zone under development in Araihazar, the Chinese Economic Zone in Anwara and several existing and new EPZs together report hundreds of factories and multibillion-dollar proposed investments. Foreign direct investment rose by 45 per cent in 2025 as global firms looked for 'China+1' alternatives. Government policy targets a 40 per cent increase in light engineering's contribution to GDP by 2027 and aims to replace a $1.3 billion annual API import bill with local production.

Every one of these sectors is far more supply-chain-intensive than the cut-and-sew process. A pharmaceutical plant must source regulated inputs from several countries, maintain traceability and pass foreign audits. An electronics assembler juggles thousands of components across multi-tier supplier networks. Getting a container through Chattogram port, customs and multiple agency approvals on time is a management discipline in itself. These industries need people who understand the supply chain end to end: complex demand and supply planning, inventory management, running complex warehouses, working out and optimising air, sea, rail and road logistics, negotiating with global suppliers, and using data analytics and AI to do all of it better. Without them, the factories in our economic zones will surely underperform, or investors will fly in their own managers, as many do today.

The clock, deferred or not

Bangladesh was scheduled to graduate from Least Developed Country (LDC) status on 24 November 2026. However, the UN General Assembly, at its most recent session, extended the preparatory period to November 2029.

When graduation occurs, duty-free access to the EU and other markets will be phased out, and tariffs on key products will rise. The only durable answer is to become efficient enough to compete without preferences. Our labour productivity is about $8.7 per hour, compared with $12.4 in Vietnam and $19.8 in China. Closing that gap is partly about machines. It is largely about skilled management.

An extension is not a reprieve. It is three years, exactly the time it takes to build a serious graduate programme and graduate its first class.
Students and instructors examine textile machinery at the BUBT textile laboratory. As Bangladesh expands into technical textiles and other industries, it needs professionals who understand complex supply chains, from production planning and inventory management to logistics. File Photo.

What our universities offer today

Bangladesh's private universities have grown impressively, but their supply chain offerings are limited. AIUB has an Operations and Supply Chain Management department offering BBA and MBA concentrations. BRAC University has a Master's in Procurement & Supply Management (MPSM) programme. A few others offer MBA majors with courses on supply chain management.

There is not a single dedicated, industry-facing master's degree (MS) in supply chain management in the country. Meanwhile, our best BBA and MBA graduates gravitate towards banks, telecoms and marketing, or jobs abroad. A factory or manufacturing company is rarely seen as a career destination for the brightest. That has created a huge talent gap.

Others have noticed. Malaysia's UCSI University already markets its supply chain master's programme directly to Bangladeshi students. When a foreign university is selling into your market, the demand is real, and the first-mover advantage for local universities will quickly disappear.

What our competitors did

Malaysia partnered with MIT's Center for Transportation and Logistics to create the Malaysia Institute for Supply Chain Innovation, whose 10-month master's programme was ranked first in the world by Eduniversal in 2021. India runs dedicated supply chain MBAs at IIM Udaipur and IIM Mumbai, backed by its National Logistics Policy.

Vietnam offers a warning. It has many bachelor's programmes, yet its own industry reports that only 5–7 per cent of its logistics workforce has formal training.

The leading US programmes at MIT, Michigan State, Arizona State, the University of Tennessee and USC share a common approach: a real capstone project with a sponsoring company, end-to-end coverage from procurement to analytics, small cohorts, and AI woven into core courses. Writing the syllabus is the easy part. Building the industry partnerships that turn capstones into hiring pipelines is the hard part, and here Bangladesh has an unusual advantage. Hundreds of investors are setting up inside our economic zones right now. A programme built around capstone partnerships with those companies would be distinctive from day one.

Three asks of university leadership

First, decide. Several private universities are well placed. Some have the brand and accreditation record to meet international standards; some already offer supply-chain-related degrees or courses. What is missing is not capacity but a vice-chancellor or dean willing to take ownership of the programme and build a centre of excellence in operations and supply chain management.

Second, borrow credibility. Partner with an established international programme rather than start from zero. And tap into the diaspora: senior Bangladeshi-origin supply chain academics teach in Australia and the UK, and at least one has already come home to lead a university here.
Workers operate machinery inside a factory at the Korean Export Processing Zone in Anwara and West Patiya, Chattogram. Ready-made garments account for 80–83 percent of Bangladesh's exports and employ some 4.4 million people, but the country's emerging industries will require far more complex supply chain management. Photo: Star

Third, start the clock. Getting from a firm decision to the first graduating cohort takes roughly 32–36 months: about three months to commit, six months to design the curriculum and submit it to the UGC, four months to secure approval, hire faculty and sign up capstone sponsors, followed by an 18-month programme.

Government policymakers and industry have roles too. BIDA has streamlined the investment process through Invest Bangladesh. Invest Bangladesh should now treat professional talent as investment infrastructure, as Thailand did with its Eastern Economic Corridor, by offering co-funded scholarships and tax incentives for companies that sponsor students. Manufacturers who complain about the skills gap should sponsor capstone projects and hire graduates of these programmes. Nor is this a job for private universities alone: BUET and the larger public universities should also take the coming talent gap seriously and begin developing their own plans.

Why now

The new deadline for LDC graduation is November 2029. A university that commits this year can graduate its first cohort in early 2030, just as preferences begin to lapse and the economic zones reach scale. If we can supply only blue-collar labour to these economic zones, and not the professionals who run them, the whole diversification effort will stall before it starts.

We have proven we can make clothes for the world. The question now is whether we can manage the far more complex supply chains our new industries demand, or whether we will keep importing the talent.

Reza Kibria is an independent adviser to NGOs, higher education institutions and start-ups. He has three decades of supply chain management experience with US multinational companies and, most recently, spent five years with the USC Marshall School of Business in Los Angeles.
