item.title: The Daily Star – Maulana Bhashani in Assam, 1928–1947 : Peasants in the national liberation movement
item.description:
‘The peasantry is systematically disregarded for the most part by the propaganda put out by the nationalist parties.’ (Fanon, 1990: 47)

Frantz Fanon (1925–1961) participated in Algeria’s struggle for independence. Long before the Liberation War of 1971, the peasants of Bangladesh had experienced much the same thing. A consideration of Maulana Abdul Hamid Khan Bhashani’s life also compels us to acknowledge the truth of Fanon’s observation. In this brief essay, I shall confine myself to highlighting this particular lesson.

The life of Maulana Bhashani is, in a sense, the story of Bangladesh’s Muslim peasantry, commonly known as Bengali Muslims.

By a stroke of fortune, he remained largely beyond the reach of colonial education. It seems that the corrupting influence of that education could not entirely diminish his extraordinary character. On numerous occasions, he unmasked the principal comprador or collaborating classes, including landlords, the newly wealthy and the middle classes. He began this work long before the Partition of India, in the province of Assam in undivided India. His name remains unforgettable among the leading figures of the struggle for independence achieved in 1947.

Yet Maulana Bhashani’s contribution to the struggle for independence in 1947 was, in one way or another, erased from the histories written in subsequent decades. This was true not only in the new India but also in the newly established Pakistan. Indeed, apart from a handful of scattered essays, his achievements have remained largely unknown to the wider public to this day.

In this essay, I shall offer only a brief account of Maulana Bhashani’s life, particularly his political career, which began in the province of Assam in undivided India. A comprehensive examination of all its dimensions lies beyond the scope of my knowledge.

I

In 1971, faced with attacks by the Pakistani military, Maulana Bhashani sought refuge in India. Among those who accompanied him was Saiful Islam, a left-wing political activist from the Pabna–Sirajganj region. Indeed, during their wartime exile, he also served as the Maulana’s personal assistant. In 1987, he published some of his recollections and experiences in a volume entitled Swadhinata Bhashani Bharat (Independence, Bhashani and India). About a decade and a half later, around 2002, he published another booklet with the rather cumbersome title Assam O Maulana Bhashani Ebong Line Protha-Bangalkheda (Assam, Maulana Bhashani, the Line System and the Expulsion of Bengalis). This booklet, too, drew upon his experiences of 1971. In it, he attributed many statements directly to Maulana Bhashani, although he did not always specify where or when the Maulana had made them.

As I began reading the booklet, I found myself confronted with a question: Why, and for what reasons, had Maulana Bhashani joined the Pakistan Movement? The answer is not straightforward. Nor does Saiful Islam offer any particularly illuminating answer to this question. I recalled that he, too, belonged to those generally described as leftists in our country. Regrettably, I found that only by carefully considering his various observations might one arrive at something resembling an answer.
Maulana Abdul Hamid Khan Bhashani attends a meeting of the advisory committee of the Bangladesh government-in-exile during the Liberation War of 1971, alongside Tajuddin Ahmad, Professor Muzaffar Ahmad, Monoranjan Dhar, Comrade Moni Singh and other leaders.

Saiful Islam frequently made a point of telling others that, although he enjoyed a good personal relationship with Maulana Bhashani, he did not consider the Maulana’s politics to be correct. At one point in his booklet, Maulana Bhashani O Assam Ebong Line Protha-Bangalkheda, Saiful Islam writes explicitly:

‘I could not agree with him about the involvement of religion in discussion, reasoning, movements, rebellions and revolutions. It was for this reason that, despite having a good personal relationship with Maulana Bhashani, I could not remain politically associated with him’ (Islam, 2003: 25).

Now, in 1971, while Bangladesh’s Liberation War was under way, Saiful Islam asked Maulana Bhashani, as they sat on the soil of Bhashan Char in Assam: ‘Why did you transform the non-communal movement against the Line System in Assam into the communal Pakistan Movement?’ In response, Maulana Bhashani invoked the egalitarian and other positive dimensions of religion.

Saiful Islam had his own convictions. Why would he listen to arguments about religion? The problem lay within his own assumptions. Even before posing the question, he already knew what he expected the answer to be. He had taken it for granted that ‘Pakistan’ was a ‘communal’ phenomenon, or merely another name for communalism. He had no real interest in discovering whether there was anything more to it.

It is true that he did not receive the answer he had hoped for. Yet another kind of answer presented itself to him through an actual event. He failed, however, to recognise that the event itself contained an answer to his question. The Pakistan Movement was not merely a communal movement; it was also a form of national movement.

An examination of the experience of the broad-based popular movement organised under Maulana Bhashani’s leadership to abolish the Line System, introduced by the British colonial government to restrict the settlement of Bengali Muslim peasants in Assam, would likewise demonstrate that the parties leading, or claiming to lead, struggles for national independence have consistently been reluctant to recognise peasant movements as either the foundation of, or participants in, national movements.

Saiful Islam recounts that, at one point during their stay in a refugee camp in India in 1971, Maulana Bhashani expressed a personal wish. He wanted to meet his disciples one last time. There was only one way to bring thousands of his disciples together: to organise an urs, a religious gathering.

According to Saiful Islam’s account, arrangements were made to hold the urs at Bhashan Char. Throughout the night, the disciples engaged in zikr and other devotional recitations. The following day, a vast public gathering took place, with Maulana Bhashani as its sole speaker. Addressing the assembled disciples, followers and members of the wider public, he described the appalling acts of irreligion committed by the Pakistanis in the name of religion. At the same time, he made a point of emphasising the secular character of Bangladesh’s national struggle, that is, its universal appeal.

I have summarised Saiful Islam’s testimony above in my own customary language. I shall now reproduce his observations in his own words:

‘I came to understand that Muslims in India were not supportive of Bangladesh’s struggle for independence, both from my travels through Calcutta, Cooch Behar, Delhi, Dehradun, Ajmer and other places, and from my experiences in Assam. But during Maulana Bhashani’s speech, as I moved around the public gathering, listening to conversations among his disciples of different ages, I repeatedly heard one sentiment expressed: “Huzur wanted Pakistan, so we voted for Pakistan. Now that he no longer wants Pakistan, there must be some deeper wisdom in this.” After the public meeting, I saw that the people departed with an anti-Pakistan outlook’ (Islam, 2003: 25).
This undated photo shows Maulana Bhashani holding a portrait of Lenin. Source:sputnikimages.com

II

Everyone knows that Maulana Bhashani’s original name was Abdul Hamid Khan. Where did this name come from? Those familiar with what is known as the ‘Bengali Muslim mind’ will know that he was named after the Ottoman Sultan Abdul Hamid II, whom Bengali Muslims regarded as the Caliph of Islam. We cannot say with certainty whether Maulana Bhashani was born in 1880 or 1885. We can, however, say that our Abdul Hamid’s life began during the reign of the Ottoman Sultan-Caliph Abdul Hamid II (1876–1909). As for the name by which he became famous throughout the world, ‘Bhashani’, he acquired it from Bhashan Char in Goalpara district of Assam. He was indebted to Assam not merely for the name ‘Bhashani’, but also for his life, youth, wealth and honour. And the people of Bangladesh, in turn, owe him a debt for the independence achieved in 1947.

Who, in principle, can be regarded as the true leader of Bengali Muslims? Before any other name comes to mind, there is that of Maulana Abdul Hamid Khan Bhashani.

This is no small matter. Around the time of his birth, poor peasants from northern Bengal had begun migrating to Assam, particularly the Brahmaputra Valley, where they cultivated previously uncultivated land and established new settlements. This migration was directly connected to British colonial rule. Of those who embarked upon this arduous and hazardous undertaking with the encouragement of the British ruling authorities, the overwhelming majority, an estimated 85 per cent, were Muslims from eastern Bengal.

In 1905, Assam was joined with Eastern Bengal to form a new province. It should be remembered that 30 years earlier, in 1874, Sylhet district had been separated from Bengal and incorporated into Assam. I have heard many emotionally inclined writers describe this event as the ‘first partition of Bengal’. Even after the province of Eastern Bengal and Assam was abolished in 1911, the Muslim-majority district of Sylhet remained part of Assam. As everyone knows, the whole of Sylhet district remained within Assam until 1947. Karimganj subdivision remains in Assam to this day.

Assam’s long-established Assamese Muslim community constituted a minority. Even before the twentieth century, the Muslim population of Assam had begun to grow across both the Brahmaputra Valley in the west and the Surma Valley in the east. This development provoked two kinds of reaction: one from Assam’s established population and the other from the British rulers, particularly the owners of tea plantations. The growing Bengali Muslim population in Assam came to be perceived as a new threat.

Around 1916, discussions began about whether restrictions could be imposed to prevent peasants from eastern Bengal from settling throughout Assam. In 1920, a regulation was introduced under which designated lines or boundaries were drawn in certain districts. Peasants arriving from Bengal were prohibited from settling beyond these lines. This was the famous Line System.

Long before this, towards the end of the nineteenth century, an Assamese movement had emerged in Assam. Leaders of the Assamese community sought to establish Assamese as the medium of instruction in schools and colleges. There is evidence that the British government enthusiastically supported these efforts.

Assamese is by no means a recently developed language. Assamese prose had developed long before Bengali prose. It is a rich and mature language. There were historical connections between modern Assamese and Bengali, sustained by social interaction between the two regions. Under British rule, however, competition and rivalry emerged between the two provinces, giving rise to tensions. After 1920, this regional conflict gradually assumed communal and racially discriminatory characteristics. How this transformation occurred deserves closer examination.

Bengal and Assam were neighbouring provinces. Bengal was densely populated, a region that economists and business interests would later describe as possessing an almost unlimited supply of labour, meaning cheap labour. Assam, on the other hand, was regarded as a land-rich province. There was no shortage of uncultivated land in Assam.

The British government in India assumed that the movement of labour and access to land between the two provinces was a natural development. One province had land, while the other had workers. Together, Assam and Bengal could form an ideal combination.

Moreover, for seven years, from 1905 to 1911, the two regions were administered as a single province. Dhaka, in Eastern Bengal, became the capital of this new province. It was considered ‘natural’ that Assam’s middle classes would move to the towns and commercial centres of Eastern Bengal, while peasants from Eastern Bengal would migrate to the uncultivated lands of the Surma and Brahmaputra valleys, cultivate them and increase food production. The only factors regarded as unnatural and regrettable were differences of language, religion and class.

It was the Muslim identity of the Bengali peasants who migrated to Assam that proved to be their misfortune. This gave the Assamese nationalist movement a racial and communal character. After 1920, extremist nationalist organisations such as the Asom Jatiya Mahasabha emerged under the leadership of intellectuals including Ambikagiri Raichoudhury.

III

The struggle of Bengali Muslim peasants against the Line System introduced by the Assam government began for understandable reasons. They were simply demanding the rights of ordinary citizens. Initially, the movement was weak. A division persisted between Bengali Muslims and Assamese Muslims. Many members of the province’s Muslim elite did not look favourably upon the Bengali Muslims from Eastern Bengal, whom they regarded as uncultured or only partially cultured. They disparagingly referred to the newcomers as ‘Mymensinghias’ and ‘Bangals’. Nor did they wholeheartedly welcome the expansion of settlements by these Bengali peasants. He transformed the numerical strength of the peasantry into a formidable collective force. With the support of these peasants, Maulana Bhashani was elected a member of the Assam Provincial Legislative Assembly, the equivalent of a member of parliament today.

Having been expelled from Bengal for political reasons, he was, in a sense, compelled to enter the political battlefield of Assam. Living among the Bengali Muslim migrants there, he became involved in their movement. How did this happen? Saiful Islam recorded an account in Maulana Bhashani’s own words that offers an answer. He writes:

‘In 1929, he established his right to permanent residence in Assam by building a hut at Char Bhashan (Ghaghamari) for one taka and fourteen annas. The story of how he came to Assam and became involved in politics can be understood from his own account.’

During the first phase of the movement, he convened a peasant conference at Char Bhashan. At the time, traders in Assam used various kinds of weights and measures in commercial transactions. By manipulating these weights, upper-caste Hindu moneylenders and traders extensively cheated lower-caste Hindus and members of the hill communities. At the conference, Maulana Bhashani demanded an end to fraudulent weighing practices. As a result of Bhashani’s campaign for standardised weights, all weights other than the 80-tola seer were declared illegal in Assam and gradually disappeared from use (Islam, 2003: 16).

Among the other demands raised at the conference was an end to the oppression perpetrated by Raja Prabhat Kumar Barua of Gauripur. Through the Goalpara district administration, the Raja secured an order prohibiting the conference. Maulana Bhashani challenged the prohibition in the Calcutta High Court and won. The conference was successfully held. Abul Kasem Fazlul Huq himself represented the Maulana as his lawyer before the Calcutta High Court. He also attended the conference as its chief guest, quite literally ‘gracing’ the occasion with his presence. By this time, Maulana Bhashani’s reputation had spread to ‘every corner of Assam’. In the general elections held in 1937 under the Government of India Act 1935, he was elected to the Provincial Legislative Assembly.

The mass movement against the Line System now entered the legislative assembly itself. In 1937, the 108-member Assam Provincial Legislative Assembly was divided among ten political groups. The distribution of seats was as follows: ‘Congress 32, Muslim League 4, Assam Valley United People’s Party 8, Progressive Party 12, European Group 13, Independent Party 4, Constitutionalist Party 4, Assam Valley Muslim Group 13, Surma Valley United Muslim Party 17, and one independent member’ (Islam, 2003: 17).

Manowar Ali, an assembly member elected on the ticket of the Surma Valley United Muslim Party, introduced a motion demanding the abolition of the Line System. Abdul Matin Chowdhury of the Muslim League supported the proposal. Maulana Bhashani, an independent member and the leading figure in the movement against the Line System, also participated in the assembly debate. Outside the assembly, he called for a broad-based popular movement to achieve swaraj, or self-rule, bringing together Hindus and Muslims, Bengalis and hill communities alike.

Under the separate electorate system in the 1937 elections, Muslims were allocated 34 of the 108 seats in the Assam Legislative Assembly. Of these, as we have already seen, the Muslim League held only four. When Maulana Bhashani, initially elected as an independent, joined the Muslim League, its strength increased to five seats.

Syed Mohammad Saadulla, a member of Assam’s Muslim elite, also joined the Muslim League, although for a different reason. He was to become the Premier, while Maulana Bhashani was elected president of the Muslim League.

Following Maulana Bhashani’s example, leaders of the Assam Valley Muslim Group and the Surma Valley United Muslim Party gradually joined the Muslim League. Under Bhashani’s leadership, the Assam Provincial Muslim League became the sole political organisation representing Assam’s Muslims. The movement to abolish the Line System thus laid the foundations for the establishment of the Muslim League in Assam.

It must be remembered, however, that Bhashani’s Muslim League did not see eye to eye with the All-India Muslim League on a number of issues. Nor did he agree with Syed Saadulla, the Premier from his own party. Saiful Islam writes:

‘After the fall of the Bordoloi ministry and the formation of the Saadulla ministry, Maulana Bhashani understood that this government would not be able to abolish the Line System or put a complete end to the Bangal Kheda campaign. He also realised that the only difference between Saadulla and Bordoloi was one of the cap and the tiki [the traditional Hindu hair tuft]. The fall of Bordoloi and the return of Saadulla could, at most, lead to some relaxation in the strict enforcement of the Line System’ (Islam, 2003: 21).

Between 1937 and 1947, at least six governments were formed in Assam. The province also experienced a period of Governor’s Rule. Syed Saadulla of the Muslim League and Gopinath Bordoloi of the Congress alternately formed governments. There was, of course, no question of the Bordoloi government abolishing the Line System. But even after repeatedly forming governments, Saadulla did not dare to abolish it either. The Bordoloi government, meanwhile, moved to suppress the movement with even greater severity. During this period, the increasingly militant slogan of ‘Bangal Kheda’ laid the groundwork for ever more extensive eviction campaigns.

Meanwhile, Maulana Bhashani continued his movement against the Line System both inside the assembly and outside it, through conferences, public meetings and political organisations. His differences with Saadulla could no longer be concealed. The All-India Muslim League offered verbal support to the peasant movement led by Bhashani, but it seems unlikely that its leaders genuinely endorsed it.

A single example will help illustrate the situation. On 8 and 9 February 1942, Maulana Bhashani convened the second joint Assam–Bengal Peasants’ Conference at Ghaghamari in Goalpara. He nominated the renowned independence activist Maulana Azad Sobhani as president of the conference. Renewed efforts were made to preserve and enforce the system.

Following the February 1944 conference, the Saadulla ministry decided that, in the reserved grazing lands of districts such as Nowgong, Kamrup and Darrang, five bighas of land would be retained for each buffalo and another five bighas for every three cattle, while the remaining land would be distributed among the landless. ‘On 3 May 1947, during a session of the Bengal Provincial Legislative Assembly, Nur Ahmed introduced a private member’s motion urging the central government to abolish the Line System and put an end to the Bangal Kheda campaign. The motion provoked a heated debate between the government and opposition members in the assembly.

‘Amid the exchanges between the Muslim League and Congress, Communist Party member Comrade Jyoti Basu expressed his opinion. He argued that it was deeply shameful that Bengal, instead of providing food for its own children, was pushing them into other regions and provinces. The source of the problem lay in Bengal’s land system. The problem should be resolved by transforming the system of landownership and distribution through a successful united struggle to overthrow its creators and protectors: the landlords, moneylenders and the British’ (Islam, 2003: 47–48).

The movement to abolish the Line System failed to secure support even from the Communist Party of India itself, let alone from other political forces.

By manipulating these weights, upper-caste Hindu moneylenders and traders extensively cheated lower-caste Hindus and members of the hill communities. As a result of Bhashani’s campaign for standardised weights, all weights other than the 80-tola seer were declared illegal in Assam and gradually disappeared from use (Islam, 2003: 16).

Among the other demands raised at the conference was an end to the oppression perpetrated by Raja Prabhat Kumar Barua of Gauripur. Through the Goalpara district administration, the Raja secured an order prohibiting the conference. Maulana Bhashani challenged the prohibition in the Calcutta High Court and won. The conference was successfully held. Abul Kasem Fazlul Huq himself represented the Maulana as his lawyer before the Calcutta High Court. He also attended the conference as its chief guest, quite literally ‘gracing’ the occasion with his presence. By this time, Maulana Bhashani’s reputation had spread to ‘every corner of Assam’. In the general elections held in 1937 under the Government of India Act 1935, he was elected to the Provincial Legislative Assembly.

The mass movement against the Line System now entered the legislative assembly itself. In 1937, the 108-member Assam Provincial Legislative Assembly was divided among ten political groups. The distribution of seats was as follows: ‘Congress 32, Muslim League 4, Assam Valley United People’s Party 8, Progressive Party 12, European Group 13, Independent Party 4, Constitutionalist Party 4, Assam Valley Muslim Group 13, Surma Valley United Muslim Party 17, and one independent member’ (Islam, 2003: 17).

Manowar Ali, an assembly member elected on the ticket of the Surma Valley United Muslim Party, introduced a motion demanding the abolition of the Line System. Abdul Matin Chowdhury of the Muslim League supported the proposal. Maulana Bhashani, an independent member and the leading figure in the movement against the Line System, also participated in the assembly debate. Outside the assembly, he called for a broad-based popular movement to achieve swaraj, or self-rule, bringing together Hindus and Muslims, Bengalis and hill communities alike.

Under the separate electorate system in the 1937 elections, Muslims were allocated 34 of the 108 seats in the Assam Legislative Assembly. Of these, as we have already seen, the Muslim League held only four. When Maulana Bhashani, initially elected as an independent, joined the Muslim League, its strength increased to five seats.

Syed Mohammad Saadulla, a member of Assam’s Muslim elite, also joined the Muslim League, although for a different reason. He was to become the Premier, while Maulana Bhashani was elected president of the Muslim League.

Following Maulana Bhashani’s example, leaders of the Assam Valley Muslim Group and the Surma Valley United Muslim Party gradually joined the Muslim League. Under Bhashani’s leadership, the Assam Provincial Muslim League became the sole political organisation representing Assam’s Muslims. The movement to abolish the Line System thus laid the foundations for the establishment of the Muslim League in Assam.

It must be remembered, however, that Bhashani’s Muslim League did not see eye to eye with the All-India Muslim League on a number of issues. Nor did he agree with Syed Saadulla, the Premier from his own party. Saiful Islam writes:

‘After the fall of the Bordoloi ministry and the formation of the Saadulla ministry, Maulana Bhashani understood that this government would not be able to abolish the Line System or put a complete end to the Bangal Kheda campaign. He also realised that the only difference between Saadulla and Bordoloi was one of the cap and the tiki [the traditional Hindu hair tuft]. The fall of Bordoloi and the return of Saadulla could, at most, lead to some relaxation in the strict enforcement of the Line System’ (Islam, 2003: 21).

Between 1937 and 1947, at least six governments were formed in Assam. The province also experienced a period of Governor’s Rule. Syed Saadulla of the Muslim League and Gopinath Bordoloi of the Congress alternately formed governments. There was, of course, no question of the Bordoloi government abolishing the Line System. But even after repeatedly forming governments, Saadulla did not dare to abolish it either. The Bordoloi government, meanwhile, moved to suppress the movement with even greater severity. During this period, the increasingly militant slogan of ‘Bangal Kheda’ laid the groundwork for ever more extensive eviction campaigns.

Meanwhile, Maulana Bhashani continued his movement against the Line System both inside the assembly and outside it, through conferences, public meetings and political organisations. His differences with Saadulla could no longer be concealed. The All-India Muslim League offered verbal support to the peasant movement led by Bhashani, but it seems unlikely that its leaders genuinely endorsed it.

A single example will help illustrate the situation. On 8 and 9 February 1942, Maulana Bhashani convened the second joint Assam–Bengal Peasants’ Conference at Ghaghamari in Goalpara. He nominated the renowned independence activist Maulana Azad Sobhani as president of the conference. A resolution was adopted declaring that unless the Line System was abolished and Bangal Kheda stopped by 3 March 1942, the movement would adopt a resolution calling for the abolition of landlordism and launch a boycott. Following this declaration, not only the British government and the Congress but also the central leadership of the Muslim League refused to support Bhashani.

At the Muslim League conference held in Barpeta district of Assam on 7 and 8 April 1944, Maulana Bhashani was once again elected president. Another resolution demanding the abolition of the Line System was adopted. Even then, the Saadulla government did not abolish it. During this period, the British government and Congress leaders began portraying the movement against the Line System as a strategy to increase the Muslim population of Assam. Renewed efforts were made to preserve and enforce the system.

Following the February 1944 conference, the Saadulla ministry decided that, in the reserved grazing lands of districts such as Nowgong, Kamrup and Darrang, five bighas of land would be retained for each buffalo and another five bighas for every three cattle, while the remaining land would be distributed among the landless. In certain areas, the boundaries drawn by British officials under the Line System were relaxed or removed. This created opportunities for the Bengali Muslim population to increase in the lower-lying areas of Assam. Taking advantage of what they regarded as an alarming situation, Congress leaders renewed their demands for strict enforcement of the Line System, which had by then weakened somewhat.

On 16 December 1944, an all-party conference was convened at the initiative of Gopinath Bordoloi and Syed Saadulla to resolve disputes over land administration. Among its decisions was a resolution stipulating that only those who had arrived in Assam from outside the province before 1 January 1938, that is, by 31 December 1937, would be considered eligible for land settlement.

Maulana Bhashani and his supporters refused to accept this proposal. They demanded that land be distributed among all those who had arrived in Assam up to 1940. They also insisted that the accursed Line System should eventually be abolished altogether.

Congress leaders, too, disagreed with several resolutions adopted at the all-party conference. They argued that the conference had failed to protect the interests of lower-caste Hindus, hill communities or ‘tribal’ populations, Assamese cattle and buffalo herders, and grass cutters.

In response to these objections from Congress, the Saadulla government attempted to reach a compromise with Congress and other assembly members in March 1945. These efforts culminated in the Tripartite Agreement adopted on 13 July. Under its terms, every Bengali peasant who had arrived after 31 December 1937 was classified as an ‘infiltrator’ and became subject to eviction.

Needless to say, Maulana Bhashani rejected the agreement. He called for a non-cooperation movement and, around May 1946, began a hunger strike demanding the abolition of the Line System, an end to Bangal Kheda and the cessation of campaigns to evict Bengali peasants. He ended his hunger strike after a full 61 days.

Following another peasants’ conference at Mangaldai on 26 June 1946, Maulana Bhashani called his final public meeting in the town of Tezpur in Darrang district. The meeting was scheduled for 10 March 1947. Maulana Bhashani arrived at the gathering in disguise. Immediately after the public meeting, he was arrested.

While he remained in detention, British India was partitioned and the two new states gained independence. He was not released until November 1947. At the time, he was still president of the Assam Provincial Muslim League and a member of the Legislative Assembly. Immediately after his release, arrangements were made to send him to Eastern Bengal, now part of Pakistan, while the eviction campaign continued.

IV

Why did the movement to abolish the Line System fail? Saiful Islam believes that one of the reasons for its failure was the merging of the anti-Line System movement with the ‘communal’ slogan of achieving Pakistan. I reproduce his observations here in full:

‘Despite its enormous scale and intensity, why did the movement to abolish the Line System and suppress Bangal Kheda fail so substantially? A closer examination reveals several reasons: the movement’s inherent weaknesses; its class and regional circumstances; differences between Bhashani and Saadulla in their assessment of and participation in the movement; a shortage of funds; the lack of proper cooperation from the Muslim League high command; the merging of the anti-Line System movement with the communal slogan of achieving Pakistan; Bhashani’s arrest; the deployment of the military to suppress the movement; the partition of the country along communal lines; and the willingness of both the Muslim League and Congress to accept the bait of Partition. Because of these factors, the movement suffered defeat even after coming remarkably close to success’ (Islam, 2003: 48).

I do not possess the scholarly learning necessary to dispute Saiful Islam, but I detected a revealing implication in his criticism.

One question must surely be asked. What role did the Communist Party of India play in the movement to abolish the Line System? This party, too, propagated the views of upper-caste Bengali Hindus. Its own resolutions support this observation. On the question of resolving the problem, the party stated:

‘Bengalis must understand that there is a limit to the amount of cultivable land in Assam. Moreover, the shortage of land in Bengal cannot be remedied by using Assam’s land’ (Islam, 2003: 46–47).

They chose to preserve their social standing rather than uphold their professed principles. In the interest of protecting that standing, the Communist Party’s second resolution was even more remarkable:

‘Experience shows that merely evicting outsiders will not eliminate the danger of forcible occupation of reserved lands’ (Islam, 2003: 47).

The Communist Party’s proposed solution was more remarkable still:

‘The eviction campaign and the illegal, forcible occupation of land must be stopped immediately.’

What more can we possibly add at this point? Let us simply say, Alhamdulillah!

By now, the Communist Party’s straightforward position provides a satisfactory answer to the question of why the movement to abolish the Line System failed. Saiful Islam, an enthusiastic admirer of this position, writes:

‘On 3 May 1947, during a session of the Bengal Provincial Legislative Assembly, Nur Ahmed introduced a private member’s motion urging the central government to abolish the Line System and put an end to the Bangal Kheda campaign. The motion provoked a heated debate between the government and opposition members in the assembly.

‘Amid the exchanges between the Muslim League and Congress, Communist Party member Comrade Jyoti Basu expressed his opinion. He argued that it was deeply shameful that Bengal, instead of providing food for its own children, was pushing them into other regions and provinces. The source of the problem lay in Bengal’s land system. The problem should be resolved by transforming the system of landownership and distribution through a successful united struggle to overthrow its creators and protectors: the landlords, moneylenders and the British’ (Islam, 2003: 47–48).

The movement to abolish the Line System failed to secure support even from the Communist Party of India itself, let alone from other political forces.
